planting.note: Direct sow with 2-4 weeks cold-moist stratification into fast-draining sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; water sparingly after establishment, since overwatering causes lank growth and crown rot.

directions: Forming attractive gray-green mats topped with large, fragrant white flowers that fade pink, this evening primrose is extremely drought tolerant once established and visited by more than sixty native bee species — a strong low-water groundcover for hot, dry slopes. Flowers open in late afternoon and stay open into the next morning, so site it where evening light will catch the blooms. Cutting back spent flowering stems in late summer keeps the mat tidy and encourages a tighter second flush.

planting.note: Sow seed on the soil surface, since it needs light to germinate, into well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; deadhead spent capsules before they shatter to control vigorous self-sowing.

directions: A dramatic architectural biennial, forming a basal rosette the first year and three-to-eight-foot flowering spikes of large yellow blooms the second, this evening primrose is a major larval host for sphinx moths and draws hummingbirds and goldfinches. It tolerates nearly any garden soil, including compacted or clay ground, making it useful for difficult transitional spots between cultivated beds and wilder margins. The towering flower spikes are best staked or planted among sturdier neighbors in windy sites.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into fast-draining sandy or gravelly desert soil; skip supplemental fertilizer, since rich soil produces lush, short-lived rosettes with fewer flowers.

directions: A true low-desert winter annual, this evening primrose grows as a stemless rosette hugging the ground that erupts with large, fragrant yellow flowers fading to orange-red, valuable for xeric and desert-wildflower plantings where it supports specialist moths like the Pacific green sphinx. It germinates on a winter-rain cue and resents being transplanted out of its taproot. Expect the whole rosette to collapse and set seed by late spring as desert heat arrives; leave spent plants in place to self-sow.

planting.note: Direct-sow with 4-8 weeks cold stratification into sharply drained, mineral-rich gravelly soil in full sun; the thick taproot does not transplant well once established.

directions: A distinctive stemless, taprooted rosette from Sierra Nevada pumice meadows, this evening primrose carries glowing yellow flowers fading to red, a genuine high-elevation rock-garden specialist filling a niche none of the garden's lowland Oenothera cover. Because the rosette lies flat with no true stem, keep it free of mulch or overhanging companions that would shade it out. It is best suited to scree or alpine-trough rock gardens in cold-winter climates rather than mild lowland gardens, where summer humidity is its biggest threat.

planting.note: Direct-sow with cold-moist stratification, or divide dormant rhizomes, into lean, sandy or rocky well-drained soil; give it room or contain with a buried barrier, since it spreads by rhizome.

directions: A cold-hardy, rhizomatous Great Plains perennial with large white, yellow-throated flowers that open at dusk, this evening primrose tolerates poorer soil than most garden perennials and resents heavy, wet clay. The moth-pollinated flowers open at dusk and close by mid-morning, so site it where it will be seen and smelled in the evening, near a patio or path used after sundown. It combines well with other short-grass prairie natives that share its need for lean soil and minimal supplemental water.

planting.note: Sow outdoors in late fall for natural winter stratification, or cold-stratify indoors 4-8 weeks before spring sowing, into lean, fast-draining rocky or sandy soil in full sun.

directions: A tufted, nearly stemless high-elevation perennial bearing slender-tubed, bright yellow flowers over deeply toothed rosette foliage, this evening primrose has a very wide native range across the Rockies, Great Basin, and northern Plains into Canada. It is adapted to open, competition-free alpine and sagebrush-steppe ground and will be overrun by lusher companions in rich garden soil. Its tight rosette habit and evening-opening flowers make it a good choice tucked into scree beds or gravel paths where its late-day bloom can be appreciated up close.
